memories.memory_text: I remember that customer getting angry with me at the dealership because he claimed we had a deal without the TruCoat, but I was just trying to explain how it could save him money on oxidation problems, and he kept saying I was wasting his time.
I remember the customer yelling at me, accusing me of lying about the car price and the TruCoat, saying we had a deal without it and that I was wasting his and his wife's time.
I talked to my boss and managed to get a $100 discount on the TruCoat, which was the best I could do to make things right with the customer.
I remember Wade calling me to say that Stan Grossman was interested in my proposal and wanted to talk about funding at 2:30.
I got a call from Wade telling me that Stan Grossman was interested in my proposal, and I remember thinking I’d need the cash quickly to close the deal, so I made sure to note the meeting at 2:30.
I asked Shep for another way to get in touch with Carl because I was in a tight spot with special circumstances, but he just said no, and I couldn't reach those guys from Fargo at all.
I walked into Wade's office and greeted both him and Stan, knowing this meeting about the $750,000 deal could change everything for me.
When Wade asked me about my finder's fee, I was completely caught off guard and said, 'My fee? Wade, what the heck're you talkin' about?' because I hadn't expected that question at all.
I realized right then that Wade and Stan thought I was bringing them an investment opportunity, not asking for a loan, and the whole tone of the room shifted against me.
They made it clear they wouldn't give me a loan under my terms, with Stan saying, 'We're not just going to give you seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars,' and I knew the deal was falling apart.

I came out after the meeting and started scraping the ice off my windshield, but I got so angry I went into a frenzy, banging the scraper against the car, and then I just stood there, staring at nothing, frozen in place.
I called out for my wife, saying 'Hon?' twice, because I was unsettled by the mess and needed to know she was there.

I came home with groceries and saw the shower curtain on the floor, then noticed the window was open with snow drifting in, and when I checked the sink, the medicine tube was out of place, which made me frown and worry something was wrong.
I tried calling Wade to clear up the misunderstanding, but I couldn't get through, and it was making me more and more agitated.
I told Wade no cops — they said no cops, and I made it clear this is my deal because Jean is my wife, so I'm the one who has to handle the ransom exactly as they said.

I met with Wade and Stan at the Embers Family Restaurant to talk about the kidnapping and what to do with the ransom demands—I remember sitting there, sipping coffee, knowing they had my daughter and that a million dollars was a lot of damn money.
I saw how upset Scotty was about his mother being taken, and he kept urging me to call the police, even though we had already made other plans.
I told Scotty we had to play ball and that if anyone asked, he should say Mom is in Florida—just stick to that story to keep things under control.
I was told that Carl had been with a woman at the Celebrity Room and things got out of hand when Shep showed up—something about blood being shed, and now there are risks I didn’t sign up for.

I remember the phone calls that came in—Mike talking to Marge, then Carl calling me, and later that GMAC representative pressing me about the deal. It was a lot to juggle, and I could feel the pressure building.

I remember Carl yelling at me on the phone, telling me three people were killed in Brainerd and that the ransom was now the full $80,000—he screamed at me not to interrupt and to shut up, saying a deal was no longer a deal because blood had been shed.
I spoke with Reilly from GMAC, and I told him the vehicle IDs were in the mail, but he warned me that if they don't receive them by tomorrow, they'll send the matter to legal.
I can't stop thinking about Jean, tied up somewhere with a black hood over her head—I don't know exactly where she is, but I know she's in danger because of me.
I was on the phone after those two threatening calls, and I just lost it—I threw the phone and slammed my blotter down on the desk as hard as I could.

I remember trying to explain to Wade that the kidnappers wanted me to deliver the ransom alone, but he kept insisting on being part of it—he even slammed his hand on the table and said, 'It's my money, I'll deliver it!' When I argued, he pointed to the briefcase with a million dollars and told me this was his show now, not mine.
I remember Marge coming into my office asking me about a stolen tan Cutlass Ciera, wondering if any new vehicles had gone missing from the lot recently as part of her investigation.
After the officer left, I panicked and dialed Shep’s number, but the person on the other end didn’t understand—I just needed to talk to someone connected to him, I couldn’t wait.

I remember Carl calling me after getting beaten—his voice was raw and furious, and he gave me thirty minutes to bring the ransom money to the Dayton-Radisson parking ramp or he’d come and shoot me, my wife, and all my kids in the back of our heads. I could barely speak when he screamed 'GOT IT?' at the end.
I remember the plan was to meet at the Dayton-Radisson ramp to exchange the money for Jean, but things went wrong—I wasn't even there when Carl confronted Wade, and it turned violent.
I was driving up the ramp in my Oldsmobile when a car suddenly swerved at high speed, nearly hitting me.
I pulled up next to Wade's car and saw his body lying in the snow—I couldn't believe it, I just froze and said, 'Oh, geez!'
I dragged Wade's body through the snow to the Cadillac, opened the trunk with his keys, and I put him inside.
I retrieved the keys from the driver's side of the Cadillac and used them to open the trunk.
I kicked snow over the bloodstains to hide them.
I dragged Wade's body to the Cadillac, stuffed him in the trunk, kicked snow over the blood, and drove away, glancing toward the booth as I left.
I drove the Cadillac past the broken exit gate and saw the booth was empty except for a leg sticking out from inside, the body lying awkwardly in the snow.
I came home and went straight to the foyer chair to take off my galoshes without looking at Scott.
Scott asked me if everything was okay and whether I was going to call Stan, but I didn't feel like explaining anything to him.
I was trying to cooperate, but when she asked to speak to Mr. Gustafson, I felt she was pushing too hard and challenging my authority, so I snapped at her.
I reluctantly agreed to do the lot count right then and there, telling her I'd do a damned count and do it immediately because she just wouldn't let up.
I remember Marge pressing me, asking how I could be sure no cars were missing, like she was challenging my authority and questioning my procedures right there in front of everyone.
I just grabbed my parka and galoshes and got in my car, driving off around the corner of the building instead of finishing the lot count or the interview.
I remember Marge questioning me about the missing vehicles and dealer plates, and I could feel the tension building until I finally snapped and fled the scene.
I know Marge must have thought I was guilty or involved when I left, but I couldn't stay under that pressure any longer.
I was trying to get out through the bathroom window when the police broke into my motel room and dragged me back inside.
I was in a motel in Bismarck, trying to escape through the bathroom window when the police caught me and dragged me back inside.
I arrived in Fargo and checked into a motel, registering under the false name 'Anderson' after starting to write my real name.
I told them Shep Proudfoot said the meeting was at 8:30, even though Carl claimed it was 7:30, because I was late and needed to explain myself.
I met Carl Showalter and Gaear Grimsrud at the Jolly Troll Tavern to go over the kidnapping plan, and I handed over the keys to finalize it.
I met Carl and Gaear at the Jolly Troll Tavern to go over the kidnapping plan, and I remember saying 'okay' when we confirmed the details.
I could feel Carl's confusion when he kept asking why I'd pay ransom to myself, like the whole scheme didn't make sense to him.
Grimsrud sarcastically suggested I could just ask my wife or father-in-law for the money, as if I hadn't already thought of that.
I came home from shopping, joined my wife, son, and Wade for dinner, and tried to talk about my business deal while Wade criticized Scotty.

I asked Wade directly if he'd thought about that deal with the forty acres on Wayzata, trying to get his personal approval for the $750,000 development because I knew Stan would never sign off on it—I needed this to work out for me and Jean and Scotty.

No! No cops! That's final! This is my deal here, Wade! Jean is my wife here!
No, see, I don't need a finder's fee, I need - finder's fee's, what, ten percent, heck that's not gonna do it for me. I need the principal.
Sure right now! You're darned tootin'!
No, see, I don't need a finder'sfee, I need - finder's fee's, what, ten percent, heck that's not gonna do it for me. I need the principal.

relations.relation_summary: Jerry and Wade Gustafson share a complex and deeply antagonistic relationship rooted in both familial ties and escalating conflicts. Social relationship evidence confirms that Jerry is married to Wade's daughter Jean, making Wade his father-in-law; Jerry even addresses Wade as 'Dad,' suggesting an attempt to maintain or acknowledge the familial bond. However, this kinship is overshadowed by intense hostility. Their interactions are marked by disputes over financial arrangements, particularly a real estate deal involving forty acres on Wayzata, where Jerry pushes for immediate returns and Wade expresses skepticism and anger, indicating a breakdown in trust. The conflict intensifies around the kidnapping of Jean, where Jerry is revealed to be directly involved—possibly as a perpetrator—while simultaneously engaging with Wade about ransom demands and protection for Jean. Wade resents Jerry’s involvement, calling him unprofessional and threatening to bring in someone else, which underscores his distrust. Despite a fleeting moment where Jerry appears to align with Wade’s concern for Jean’s safety, the relationship culminates in extreme violence: Jerry is seen attacking Wade, killing him, and then dragging and concealing his body in the trunk of a Cadillac. This act represents the ultimate betrayal, transforming their strained familial and business relationship into one of fatal antagonism. The relationship does not evolve toward reconciliation but instead deteriorates from tension to murder, profoundly impacting the narrative trajectory. Jerry’s actions suggest manipulation and self-interest, using the familial connection as a cover for criminal intent.

The relationship between Jerry and Marge is defined by hostility and investigative antagonism, with Marge perceiving Jerry as a suspect in a criminal investigation. Social relationship evidence reveals repeated instances of tension, including Jerry's verbal aggression, physical resistance, and attempts to evade Marge, as well as Marge's persistent, suspicion-driven questioning. These interactions establish a power imbalance rooted in Marge's role as an investigator and Jerry's defensive, evasive behavior. The only shared event—Marge thanking Jerry and departing—appears to be a formal conclusion to an interrogation, underscoring the transactional and impersonal nature of their interaction. This moment does not indicate resolution or rapport but rather the end of a confrontational exchange. The emotional dynamic remains consistently adversarial, with no evidence of trust, cooperation, or personal connection. The relationship does not evolve beyond this antagonistic framework, and Jerry's actions suggest guilt or fear, while Marge's behavior reflects professional diligence and growing suspicion. The evidence is insufficient to confirm any underlying complexity or hidden dimensions beyond the investigative conflict.

The relationship between Jerry and the Customer is defined by sustained hostility and conflict, primarily rooted in their roles as salesperson and customer. Social relationship evidence consistently highlights antagonism, with the Customer accusing Jerry of dishonesty regarding product pricing and discounts for TruCoat, leading to escalating tension. This animosity is further demonstrated in shared events where the Customer, along with his wife, confronts Jerry at GUSTAFSON OLDS GARAGE, expressing frustration over repeated discussions and their refusal to accept the product. The emotional dynamic is marked by anger and defensiveness, culminating in the Customer yelling at Jerry in a verbally aggressive manner, demanding resolution. Jerry, in turn, attempts to defend his position, indicating stress and professional pressure. The evidence suggests no evolution toward resolution or reconciliation; instead, the relationship remains adversarial, impacting Jerry’s interactions by placing him in a reactive, defensive stance and reinforcing the Customer’s distrust. The conflict appears central to the narrative tension in their scenes.

memories.memory_text: I was asleep when the phone rang, and I answered it—heard about an incident and knew I had to respond, so I told them I'd be there in a jif.
I got a call about an incident out in the snow, so I knew I had to leave home right away to check it out.
I told Norm I had to run, but he kept offering to fix me eggs even though I didn't have time for breakfast.
I was in my uniform and had to leave the house quickly to respond to a police matter.
I exchanged loving words with Norm before I left—he said 'Love ya, Margie,' and I told him 'Love ya, hon.'
I accepted a cup of coffee from Lou because it was cold out, and I appreciated his gesture of concern.
I suddenly felt nauseous at the crime scene and had to put my head between my knees in the snow—I told Lou I was going to barf, then admitted it was just morning sickness, revealing I'm pregnant.
I was down in the ditch on my hands and knees, looking at the footprints in the snow, and I realized there were two of them—one guy smaller than the other—so I called out to Lou to let him know.
I arrived at the highway crime scene and began assessing the situation with Lou, asking him about the triple homicide involving the state trooper and the two others.
I pointed out to Lou that 'DLR' in the citation book likely stood for 'dealer plates,' not part of a license plate, and I could tell he realized his mistake when he said, 'Oh... geez.'
I gave Norm a sack of earthworms at headquarters during lunch, and he accepted them with a smile, saying thanks, hon.
I was told by Lou that two men had checked into the Blue Ox motel two nights before in a tan Ciera and left the tag space blank, which felt like a new lead worth following.
I arrived at the police headquarters during lunch, shared a meal with Norm, and discussed the case with Lou—I remember asking about the vehicle and thinking the lead from Blue Ox was a good one.
I interviewed two sex workers at a closed strip club, sitting with them on the dance platform to gather information about the suspects.

I remember Hooker Two saying the other suspect looked like the Marlboro Man, though she thought she might have been influenced because he smoked Marlboro cigarettes—a subconscious connection, she called it.
I pressed Hooker One for details about the smaller suspect, and after some hesitation, she mentioned he was uncircumcised and just generally funny-looking, which I noted as a distinctive trait.
I heard from Hooker One that the suspects mentioned going to the Twin Cities, and I acknowledged it was useful information for tracking their possible route.
I received the list of calls made from the Blue Ox motel payphone, and I noticed one of them was to Shep Proudfoot in Minneapolis.
After looking over the payphone records, I decided I'd drive down to the Twin Cities to follow up on that call to Shep Proudfoot.
Norm and I ate lunch at a cafeteria where Gary came by to deliver some information I needed for the investigation.
I checked into the Downtown Radisson Hotel and asked the clerk if there was a phone nearby and if they could recommend a good lunch spot.
I used the public phone in the hotel lobby to call Detective Sibert about my investigation and also asked him for a decent lunch place downtown.
I heard that Carl took off a license plate from a parked car up on the rooftop lot and put another one on, probably trying to hide what the car was.
I interviewed Shep Proudfoot at Gustafson Olds and warned him that helping criminals or failing to cooperate could violate his parole and send him back to prison.
I remember calling Jerry to warn him that if he didn't submit the vehicle IDs by tomorrow, we'd have to take legal action.
I asked Jerry if any vehicles had been stolen from his lot recently, specifically a tan Cutlass Ciera, because I was wondering if it might be connected to the Brainerd crimes.
After I left, I think Jerry must have tried to call Shep or someone close to him—I could sense he was getting more and more worked up.

I remember the phone ringing late at night and me groping in the dark to answer it. When Mike Yanagita called and said he saw me on the news about the Brainerd shootings, I could hear the excitement in his voice when he said, 'I can't believe it!' and asked if I was Margie Olmstead. I said, 'Mike!' and told him it was great to hear from him after all that time.
I remember Mike called me, and around the same time I heard Jerry got calls from Carl and GMAC, though I didn’t speak to any of them myself.
I met Mike Yanagita for lunch at the Radisson bar, where we caught up on old times and I told him a bit about my case, though there wasn’t much to share.

I remember Mike telling me about his wife Linda passing away from leukemia during our lunch at the Radisson bar—he seemed hesitant at first, but then shared how she had died, and I could tell it was still painful for him.
I saw Mike become so emotional during our lunch at the Radisson bar—he started weeping and admitted how lonely he'd been, especially after seeing me on TV, and it really caught me off guard.
I spoke with someone before I left that morning, checking on Mike and Linda, and I was surprised to hear he's been struggling and living with his parents, and that Linda's fine and I should call her.

I pressed Jerry on how he could be so sure no cars were missing, questioning whether he'd done any recent inventory, because it seemed like a big coincidence that the criminals used dealer plates and called someone from his dealership.
I asked Jerry if I could speak to Mr. Gustafson, trying to move the conversation forward, and that's when he suddenly exploded in anger.
Instead of finishing the lot count or even staying put, I saw Jerry grab his coat and galoshes, then drive off around the corner of the building, just leaving the interview behind.

I went back to question Jerry Lundegaard about the missing vehicles and dealer plates, and things got tense fast—he started yelling about counting, then grabbed his coat and galoshes and tried to run, easing his car around the corner of the building, and I remember muttering, 'Oh, for Pete's sake,' as he got away.
I realized he was fleeing because he felt the pressure of my questions—he must have known he was involved or guilty in some way.

I remember talking with Detective Sibert and hearing from her that Jerry and Gustafson were missing, and that Shep Proudfoot was wanted—boy, did I think then that this thing was going higher than we thought.

I met with Detective Sibert in the police cafeteria to go over what we knew, and she gave me updates on the case, including that Jerry was wanted for questioning in a triple homicide and that his wife was in the hospital with cancer, and I thanked her because her cooperation really helped.
I recall that Detective Sibert insisted on paying for both our meals, and even though I protested, she said, 'Oh, don't be silly,' in such a friendly way that I let it go.
I saw Grimsrud burst out of the cabin without a coat, ax in hand, and I watched him swing it down into Carl’s neck just as Carl was fumbling for his gun.
I remember Grimsrud using the wood chipper, forcing what was left of Carl’s body into it with a log, like he was feeding timber into a mill.

I located the cabin and stood in the cold, listening to the roar of a power tool, then moved carefully from tree to tree until I could see Grimsrud in the back lot, dismembering Carl's body in the snow; I shouted for him to stop and put his hands up, he threw a log at me and ran, so I shot him in the leg, approached with my gun drawn, cuffed him, and told him to get on his belly with his hands behind him.

I located the cabin and saw Grimsrud dismembering Carl's body; I commanded him to surrender, shot him in the leg when he tried to run, and then I arrested him, putting handcuffs on him before driving him back in the squad car.

I tried to piece together who the victims were while driving with Grimsrud—I realized Jean Lundegaard must have been the one in the cabin, and I figured the man in the wood chipper was Carl, his accomplice, along with those three others in Brainerd.

I told Grimsrud that there's more to life than money, even though he didn't respond, and I felt sorrow thinking about how all this senseless violence happened just for a little bit of cash on a beautiful day.
I was told later that law enforcement found Jerry in a motel in Bismarck and arrested him after he tried to flee through a bathroom window.
I saw on the TV that Norm's painting of a mallard was chosen for the three-cent stamp, and I couldn't believe it at first.
I kept telling Norm how proud I was of him, because I really was—his art winning that contest meant so much to me.

Norm and I were in bed together watching TV when I found out his duck painting had won the three-cent stamp contest, and I told him, 'I'm so proud a you, Norm,' because I really was, and he reached over and rested his hand on my stomach.
I saw a man in his early forties arrive and start to register under the name 'Jerry Lundega,' but then I watched him cross out the last name and change it to 'Anderson' right before my eyes.
I kept asking until Jerry finally agreed to do a lot count right then and there, and I remember him saying, 'Okay, I'll do a damned lot count!'—so I knew I got him to act.

memories.memory_text: I remember Grimsrud suddenly demanding we stop at Pancakes Hause, his voice sharp like he wasn't asking, just telling me where we were going.

I tried to talk him into skipping Pancakes Hause and going to a place outside Brainerd where we could get pancakes and then have sex with truck-stop prostitutes, and after he insisted, I agreed to it.
I was driving with Grimsrud from Brainerd to the Twin Cities, and we barely said a word the whole time—just long stretches of silence between us.
I heard Grimsrud say he needed unguent after looking at his thumb, so I knew he was hurt and wanted some kind of treatment.
I broke into the Lundegaard home with Grimsrud, we confronted Jean, and after she fought back, we managed to subdue her in a violent struggle.

I saw Jean trying to escape—she used the phone, tried to climb out the window, and hid behind the shower curtain—but I went after her and saw her get tangled, stumble out, and fall down the stairs when she tripped on the landing.
I saw Grimsrud snap at Jean, warning he'd throw her back in the trunk if she didn't stop making noise, and I knew we were all on edge.
I told Jean to stay quiet in the back seat or we'd have to shoot her, trying to keep things under control.
I noticed the trooper seemed suspicious, like he might have heard something from the back seat, and I wasn't sure if he knew she was there.
I tried to give the trooper a fifty-dollar bill to avoid getting a citation, hoping we could just handle it right there in Brainerd.

I was in the car during the traffic stop when Grimsrud reached across me, grabbed the trooper by the hair, slammed his head into the door, pulled a gun from the glove compartment, and shot him in the back of the head right in front of me.

I was driving when I heard a siren and saw flashing lights behind me; a state trooper pulled me over because my temporary tags weren't properly registered, and I watched him write something in his citation book before he approached my window.
I remember Grimsrud mocking me, saying I was smooth smooth after my attempt to bribe the trooper failed.
I heard Grimsrud order me to clear the trooper's body off the road, and I knew I had to do it.
I started to lift the body when I saw headlights coming from an oncoming car, and it stopped me cold.
I arrived at the remote lakeside cabin with Grimsrud, bringing Jean who was restrained with her hands tied and a hood over her head.
I held Grimsrud back with my hand on his shoulder and told him to wait, enjoying the sight of her struggling in the snow.
I saw her break free from Grimsrud and stumble across the snowy lawn, lurching and falling in a disoriented escape attempt.
I saw Jean Lundegaard tied to a chair with a black hood over her head.
I was banging on my damn TV, yelling at it to work because I needed a signal—anything to plug into—when I finally caught the news about the Brainerd shootings and realized Marge was involved.

I remember hearing that there had been a series of calls—Mike to Marge, me to Jerry, and GMAC to Jerry—but I only knew about my own part when I told Jerry, 'Blood has been shed,' and that we needed to move fast.
I told Jerry that three people were killed in Brainerd and that the ransom had to be the full eighty thousand now because blood had been shed and we'd taken risks.
I raised my voice at Jerry and told him not to ever interrupt me, to just shut up and stop arguing because I needed him to understand I was in control and the deal had changed.
I remember the GMAC representative calling me and warning that if I don't submit the vehicle IDs by tomorrow, they'll take legal action.
I remember how, after those two threatening calls, I just snapped—I threw my phone and slammed the blotter down on my desk, overwhelmed by rage.
I removed the license plate from a parked car on the rooftop lot and put another one on, so nobody could trace the Ciera.

I yelled at that parking attendant, calling him a pathetic piece of shit and mocking his clip-on tie because I had to pay four dollars even though I didn't park—there I was, throwing the money at him while telling him how small and meaningless his life was.
I spent time with a blonde escort at the Celebrity Room, drinking and talking before we went to the bedroom, and I was in the middle of things when Shep burst in and threw her out of bed.

I remember Shep bursting in and going wild—slapping me, punching me, slamming my head into the wall, then ripping my own belt out to choke and whip me while I gurgled on the floor. He screamed at us to get out of his house, and I barely had time to hop into my pants before he knocked me down again.

I called Jerry from a payphone after Shep beat me up, and I told him straight: get the money to the Dayton-Radisson parking ramp, top level, in thirty minutes, or I’d come for him, his wife, and all his kids—I’d shoot them all in the back of their heads. I needed him to know I meant it.
I told Wade to drop that fucking briefcase—I was done playing games, and I wasn't going to let him set the terms.

I saw Wade arrive with the ransom money and immediately start shouting about seeing his daughter before he'd hand over the briefcase, yelling 'No Jean, no money!' like he thought he could make demands.
I shot Wade in the gut when he refused to drop the briefcase after I told him to.
I saw Wade, wounded on the pavement, draw his gun and shoot me in the head at close range.
I was part of the plan to meet at the Dayton-Radisson ramp to trade the money for Jean, but it all went sideways fast.
I was hurt, blood streaming from my jaw, but I still picked up the briefcase and got in my car, peeling out to get away.
I was speeding down the ramp and swerved hard to avoid Jerry, who was coming up in his Oldsmobile.
I tried to speak to the attendant with my bleeding jaw, but my words came out muffled and unintelligible—I just needed help.
I saw Jerry drive the Cadillac past the broken gate, and I noticed the booth was empty except for a body inside with a leg sticking out awkwardly.
I drove off fast, the car roaring and kicking up snow behind me as I held the rag to my jaw.
I don't remember being there, but I heard Officer Gary Olson spoke with Mr. Mohra in his driveway about a suspicious man's threatening remarks at a bar.
I opened the briefcase and saw all that money—I couldn't believe it, I started counting and threw a bundle to the back seat, muttering to myself in shock.

I tried to remove the blood-soaked rag from my jaw, but it stuck to my skin and pulled at the wound, making me wince as the blood started flowing again, so I carefully tore the rag in half to leave only a small piece attached.

I slogged through the snow, dug a hole near a fence post with my bare hands, and buried the briefcase full of ransom money before covering it up and marking the spot with sticks because there was nothing else to distinguish it in all that white.
I laughed at Grimsrud for trying to watch that snowy, barely visible TV broadcast—he looked so stupid just sitting there.
He told me Jean started shrieking and then he killed her—I could hear the flat way he said it, like it meant nothing.
I brought all eighty grand and divided it right there, giving forty thousand to Grimsrud and keeping forty for myself.
I told Grimsrud I'm taking the Cutlass Ciera and he can have my truck—no discussion, no shared ownership, it was my call.

I lost it when Grimsrud suggested splitting the car—I called him a dummy and pulled my gun, yelling at him about listening to his bullshit for a whole week before demanding if we were square, twice, right in his face.

I came back to the cabin, my face hurting bad, laid out the money and the car keys, but Grimsrud just stared at me like I was nothing—then when I turned to leave, I heard the door and I knew something was wrong, I started reaching for my gun but he was already on me with an ax.
I walked away from the cabin thinking it was over, but then I heard the door open and turned just as Grimsrud came at me—next thing I know, he buried an ax in my neck.
I remember Jerry claiming that Shep Proudfoot told him 8:30 for the meeting, even though I knew it was supposed to be 7:30, and I figured he was just trying to justify being late.
I met Jerry Lundegaard at the Jolly Troll Tavern with Gaear to finalize the kidnapping arrangement, and I introduced both of us when he arrived.
I questioned Jerry about how it made sense for him to pay ransom to himself, because giving us forty thousand and keeping forty thousand just seemed like robbing Peter to pay Paul.
I heard Gaear sarcastically suggest that Jerry could’ve just asked his wife or father-in-law for the money instead of setting up this whole kidnapping scheme.
I saw Wade get annoyed when Scotty got up to go to McDonald's, even though he'd just eaten and hadn't finished his meal, and Wade questioned why he'd rather go out there instead.

I asked Wade if he'd thought about that real estate deal with the forty acres on Wayzata, trying to get his personal approval for the $750,000 development because I knew Stan would say no, and I needed this to work out for me and Jean and Scotty.

relations.relation_summary: The relationship between Carl Showalter and Gaear Grimsrud is defined by a complex mix of familial pretense, criminal collaboration, and escalating hostility. Social relationship evidence indicates that Carl refers to Grimsrud as 'Daddy,' suggesting either a literal father-son dynamic or a performative kinship role, possibly to reinforce their partnership or mask emotional dependency. Despite this, their interactions are marked by consistent tension: Carl repeatedly expresses frustration with Grimsrud's silence and lack of communication, culminating in verbal confrontations where he uses abusive language and threatens violence. Grimsrud responds with minimal engagement, conveying intimidation through nonverbal cues like staring and physical withdrawal, ultimately resolving the conflict through lethal force. Their collaboration is evident in multiple criminal acts, including the kidnapping of Jean Lundegaard, where they jointly exit the car, restrain the victim, and coordinate actions under Grimsrud’s direction. They are also present together during key planning stages, such as when Jerry meets with both to confirm the kidnapping arrangement. However, their partnership deteriorates over material disputes, particularly the division of a car, which triggers open arguments and mutual antagonism. This conflict reaches its apex when Grimsrud attacks and kills Carl with an ax, first striking him during a confrontation at the cabin and later disposing of his body. These events confirm a complete breakdown of their alliance, transforming their relationship from cooperative criminal associates into one of fatal hostility. The emotional dynamic shifts from strained collaboration to irreconcilable conflict, with Grimsrud asserting dominance through violence, profoundly impacting the narrative’s outcome by eliminating Carl and continuing the crime spree alone.

The relationship between Carl Showalter and Jerry is defined by escalating hostility and mutual distrust, primarily centered on the ransom money arrangement. Social relationship evidence reveals repeated confrontations where Carl exhibits verbal aggression, issues ultimatums, and physically threatens Jerry, culminating in explicit threats to kill Jerry and his family if demands are not met. This hostility is rooted in a broken agreement over the ransom split, with Carl demanding the full $80,000 and accusing Jerry of reneging on their deal. The emotional dynamic is one of fear and desperation on Jerry’s part and aggression and entitlement on Carl’s. Key events, such as Jerry explaining his financial distress to Carl and later being confronted over the phone, illustrate how their interactions deteriorate from negotiation to confrontation. The phone conversation where Jerry instructs Carl to stay away from Scotty—ending abruptly with the line going dead—marks a breakdown in communication and signals the collapse of any cooperation. These events directly impact Jerry’s behavior, pushing him toward increasingly frantic attempts to manage the situation, while Carl becomes more volatile and violent. The relationship does not evolve toward resolution but instead intensifies in conflict, ultimately reflecting a complete disintegration of trust and collaboration. The evidence is insufficient to confirm any underlying loyalty, mutual respect, or prior positive connection between the two.

The relationship between Carl Showalter and the State Trooper is defined by immediate hostility and a power imbalance rooted in law enforcement authority. The interaction begins with the trooper initiating a traffic stop due to missing vehicle tags, placing Carl in the position of a suspect under interrogation—evidenced by the trooper questioning the car's ownership. This event establishes tension and antagonism, with Carl likely perceiving the trooper as a threat to his autonomy or hidden intentions. The relationship escalates fatally, as later evidence confirms Carl is holding the trooper's body, indicating he was responsible for the trooper's death. This progression from a routine stop to a lethal outcome suggests that the confrontation profoundly impacted Carl’s trajectory, likely forcing him into further criminal behavior or flight. The emotional dynamic shifts from suspicion and authority-based stress to irreversible violence, with no indication of reconciliation or complexity beyond conflict. The relationship does not evolve beyond antagonism and ends in death.

The relationship between Carl Showalter and GRIMSRUD is defined by their joint involvement in a ransom scheme, where they cooperate to obtain and divide ransom money. This indicates a partnership rooted in mutual criminal interest and financial gain. The act of dividing the money suggests a level of trust or at least a functional working agreement between them. However, the evidence is insufficient to confirm the emotional dynamics, longevity, or evolution of their relationship beyond this collaboration. There are no shared events documented that reveal further interaction, conflict, or development in their partnership. As such, the relationship appears transactional and limited to the scope of the criminal enterprise.
